inclusion.GLOBAL_I1: Voxelwise task evidence- the analysis must be a group-level, univariate, WHOLE-BRAIN voxelwise task-evoked map. Small-volume-corrected and region-of-interest maps do NOT qualify.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I2: Task-based problem solving- the task must fit the source definition- the participant has a goal and must work out a way to reach it, applying some rule set (semantic, algebraic, logical, mechanical or other) to arrive at a previously unknown solution.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I4: Group-level effects in healthy participants. Studies comparing patients or intellectually gifted individuals to controls are eligible ONLY through their separately reported within-group healthy-control result.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I5: Stereotactic reporting- coordinates must be reported in MNI or Talairach space.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I6: How to read a sparse label- an empty or generic analysis name usually means the analysis is the only one in its table, so judge from the caption and surrounding text. A blank name is never itself a reason to exclude.

exclusion.GLOBAL_E1: DEACTIVATIONS AND REVERSE CONTRASTS- the benchmark includes only BOLD or rCBF signal INCREASES. Exclude any analysis reporting decreases, deactivations, or the reverse of a qualifying contrast (e.g. baseline > problem solving, simple > complex, trained > untrained, low > high load, rest > task). Where a paper reports a contrast in both directions, annotate only the increase direction. If the table caption or analysis name makes the direction explicit, use it; if direction is genuinely indeterminate, treat the analysis as an activation.
exclusion.GLOBAL_E2: ROI-only or small-volume-corrected analyses without whole-brain voxelwise results.
exclusion.GLOBAL_E3: Connectivity analyses- seed-based connectivity, effective connectivity (PPI, DCM) or resting-state analyses.
exclusion.GLOBAL_E4: Non-task or passive paradigms- passive viewing, simple perception, or tasks not requiring the participant to work out a solution.
exclusion.GLOBAL_E6: Between-group contrasts and group x condition interactions (patients vs controls, gifted vs controls, age or gender group comparisons). Note this is about the CONTRAST- a within-group contrast computed in a control group qualifies.

inclusion.DOMAIN_GENERAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_I1: Any analysis that satisfies the global criteria above qualifies here, regardless of representational domain. This is the pooled global network, so it is the union of the three representational domains rather than a separate construct.

inclusion.MATHEMATICAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_I1: The problem is posed with numerical stimuli and solved by manipulating numbers- arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), multi-digit or multi-step calculation, number bisection or number-line tasks, approximate or exact estimation, and the paced auditory or visual serial addition test (PASAT).
inclusion.MATHEMATICAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_I2: Domain is decided by the STIMULI, not by the reasoning involved. A complexity manipulation over arithmetic problems belongs here as well as to logical_reasoning.

exclusion.MATHEMATICAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_E1: Simple number perception, digit matching, or magnitude comparison with no problem to solve.

inclusion.VERBAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_I1: The problem is posed with letter, word or sentence stimuli and solved using logic or content knowledge. Paradigms the source paper places here- DEDUCTIVE REASONING (categorical, relational or propositional arguments; judging whether a conclusion follows from premises); verbal inductive and probabilistic reasoning; verbal analogy problems (word or letter-string analogies); riddles and insight problems; and paragraph-based word problems.
inclusion.VERBAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_I2: Deductive and logical reasoning over verbal material belongs HERE. It is a verbal paradigm in this benchmark, not a separate logical domain- do not divert it to logical_reasoning, which is a difficulty construct rather than a domain.

exclusion.VERBAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_E1: Passive reading or language comprehension with no problem to solve.

inclusion.VISUOSPATIAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_I1: The problem is posed with pictorial or spatial stimuli. Paradigms the source paper places here- visuospatial fluid reasoning (e.g. Raven's-style matrix problems); visual analogy problems; the Tower of London; and spatial navigation problem solving.

exclusion.VISUOSPATIAL_PROBLEM_SOLVING_E1: Simple visual perception, mental rotation, or matching with no problem to solve.

inclusion.LOGICAL_REASONING_I1: The contrast varies the DEMAND of the problem while holding the problem type broadly constant- harder versus easier, more versus fewer steps or relations, more versus less abstract, or a parametric or linear trend across difficulty. Examples from the benchmark- "Addition, Complex > Simple"; "Multi-Digit > Single-Digit"; "Procedural > Retrieval"; "High vs. Low g"; "2-relational vs 1-relational"; "4-target > 2-target"; "Large Problem Size > Small Problem Size"; "Main Effect of Relational Complexity"; "positive linear trend of analogical depth"; "Complex - Simple Deductions".
inclusion.LOGICAL_REASONING_I2: Any representational domain qualifies- mathematical, verbal and visuospatial demand contrasts are pooled into this single target.
inclusion.LOGICAL_REASONING_I3: Assign this IN ADDITION to the contrast's representational domain, not instead of it. A complexity contrast over arithmetic is both mathematical_problem_solving and logical_reasoning.

exclusion.LOGICAL_REASONING_E1: Contrasts of one problem TYPE against another (e.g. multiplication > addition, word > number problems) where difficulty is not what is being varied- those belong to their representational domain only.
exclusion.LOGICAL_REASONING_E2: Reverse-direction demand contrasts (simple > complex, low > high load), which are deactivations and are excluded benchmark-wide.
